ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, a light rope crosses over a smooth fixed pulley, and an acrobat is tied to each of its two ends (which may be regarded as particles). a stands on the ground, and b is on a high platform. At this time, the angle between the taut thin ropes is 60°, and the thin rope on the left side is vertical. If b starts to swing down from rest from the position shown in the figure, when b swings to the lowest point, a just has no pressure on the ground. Neglecting air resistance, then the ratio of the masses of a and b is (　　)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the upper part of the figure there is a smooth fixed pulley, and a light rope crosses over the pulley. The left rope segment is vertically downward and is connected to acrobat a standing on the ground; the right rope segment is inclined downward to the right and is connected to acrobat b standing on a high platform. In the figure, near the pulley, the angle between the left vertical rope segment and the right inclined rope segment is marked as 60°. Reasoning: Let the rope length from the pulley to b be l, the mass of b be m_b, and the mass of a be m_a. Before a has left the ground, a stands on the ground without moving, so the left-side rope length remains unchanged, and b is equivalent to making simple pendulum motion of length l around the pulley. When b swings from the initial position from rest to the lowest point, the angle between the initial rope segment and the vertical direction is 60°, so the height by which b descends is h=l(1-cos60°)=l/2. By conservation of mechanical energy: m_b g h = (1/2)m_b v^2, that is, m_b g(l/2)=(1/2)m_b v^2, obtaining v^2=gl. When b reaches the lowest point, the centripetal-force equation along the rope direction is T-m_b g=m_b v^2/l=m_b g, so T=2m_b g. At this time a just has no pressure on the ground, that is, the support force N of the ground on a is 0; for a in the vertical direction, T=m_a g. Therefore m_a g=2m_b g, obtaining m_a:m_b=2:1.
